title: Early Humans & Ancient Worlds
description: From the first humans to the great ancient civilisations: hunter-gatherers, fire and tools, cave art, farming, the first villages and cities, the Indus Valley, Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Greece and Rome — always showing how archaeology and evidence tell us what we know, and where uncertainty remains.

lessons.title: The First People
objectives: Describe how early people found food and shelter
Name early tools and fire as important discoveries
explanation: Long, long ago — many thousands of years before cities, cars or books — people lived in small groups. They hunted animals and gathered fruits, nuts and roots. We call them hunter-gatherers.
They made tools from stone, bone and wood to cut and dig. They sheltered in caves and simple huts.
Learning to control fire was a huge step: fire kept people warm, cooked food, gave light and scared away animals.

context.text: Archaeologists know about early people from stone tools, bones, remains of fires and cave paintings found at sites around the world, including India.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who hunts animals and gathers wild plants for food
something used to do a job
a hollow space in rock
flames that give heat and light

examples: A sharp stone used to cut meat.
People sitting around a fire at night.

story.title: The Family by the Fire
story.text: Long, long ago, a family sheltered in a rocky cave. The children gathered berries while the grown-ups tracked deer. At night, they sat around a crackling fire, roasting food and telling stories. The fire kept them warm and kept the wild animals away.

activities.prompt: Long ago, people got food by…
Fire helped people stay warm and cook food.

thinking: What would be hardest about living without shops?
How do you think people discovered fire?
speaking: Tell a grown-up three things early people did every day.

lessons.title: The Painted Rocks of Bhimbetka
objectives: Describe what early cave paintings show
Know paintings are evidence of how people lived
prerequisites: Knows early people lived in caves
explanation: Early people painted on rock walls. In India, the rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh have thousands of paintings made over a very long time.
The paintings show animals like deer, bison and elephants, people hunting, dancing and riding animals.
Paints were made from natural colours: red and yellow from earth and minerals, white from chalky stone. These paintings are clues about how people lived.

context.text: Bhimbetka is a UNESCO World Heritage Site; its paintings span many periods, with some among the oldest rock art in India.

vocabulary.meaning: paintings or carvings on rock
a place to stay safe
a natural substance from the earth
rock shelters with ancient paintings in Madhya Pradesh

examples: A painting of a group of people dancing in a line.
Red colour made from crushed red stone.

story.title: The Message on the Wall
story.text: Ivaan visited Bhimbetka with his parents. On the rock walls, he saw red deer leaping and tiny people dancing. "Who painted these?" he whispered. "People who lived here long, long ago," said Mama. "They couldn't write, so they left pictures. And we can still read them today."

activities.prompt: Early paints came from natural colours.

thinking: Why do you think people painted animals?
What would you paint to tell people about your life?
speaking: Describe a cave painting to a grown-up and say what it tells us.

lessons.title: When People Started Farming
objectives: Explain how farming began
Describe how farming changed the way people lived
explanation: About 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, people in some places began to plant seeds and grow crops like wheat and barley. They also tamed animals like goats, sheep and cattle. This is called domestication.
Farmers needed to stay near their fields, so they built permanent homes and lived in villages.
Farming meant more food, so villages grew. People made clay pots to store grain and water. One of the earliest farming villages in South Asia is Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan.

context.text: Archaeological evidence from Mehrgarh shows farming and herding from around 7000 BCE.

vocabulary.meaning: growing crops and raising animals
taming animals and plants for human use
a small group of homes
objects made of baked clay

examples: Grinding stones used to make flour.
Clay pots used to store grain.

story.title: The Seed That Stayed
story.text: A hunter-gatherer girl noticed that seeds dropped near the camp grew into the same plants the next year. Her family tried planting more. The harvest was good, so they stayed instead of moving on. They built mud houses, tamed a few goats, and soon their camp became a village.

activities.prompt: Farming let people stay in one place.

thinking: What new problems might farming have created?
Why did villages grow bigger?
speaking: Explain to someone why farmers built permanent homes.

lessons.title: The Wonderful Wheel
objectives: Describe important early inventions
Explain how inventions made life easier
explanation: Early people invented many things that changed life. The wheel, invented over 5,000 years ago, was used first for making pots and then for carts.
People learned to spin thread and weave cloth from cotton, wool and flax. The Indus Valley people are among the earliest known to grow cotton.
People learned to get metals from rocks. Copper came first; mixing copper with tin made bronze, which was harder — so we call this time the Bronze Age.

context.text: Archaeologists have found evidence of cotton textiles at Indus sites and early wheels and carts from Mesopotamia and other regions dating to around the 4th millennium BCE.

vocabulary.meaning: something new that people create
a round object that turns on an axle
make cloth by crossing threads
a metal made from copper and tin

examples: A potter's wheel for shaping clay.
Toy carts with wheels found at Indus sites.

story.title: The Rolling Log
story.text: Long ago, people moved heavy stones on rolling logs. One clever builder cut a slice from a log, made a hole in the middle and put a stick through. It rolled! Soon there were carts, and a potter put a wheel on its side to spin clay. One idea changed the world.

activities.prompt: The wheel was first used for…

Match the invention to its use

thinking: Which invention do you think changed life the most?
How would you move a heavy object without wheels?
speaking: Show someone how a wheel and axle make moving things easier.

lessons.title: Amazing Planned Cities
objectives: Describe features of Harappan cities
Explain how we know about them
explanation: The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation flourished around 2600–1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan and north-western India. Its major cities included Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira and Lothal.

The cities were carefully planned: straight streets in a grid, houses of baked bricks of standard sizes, and covered drains — a sanitation system remarkable for its time. Mohenjo-daro had a large public "Great Bath".
Lothal in Gujarat had a dockyard-like structure, suggesting trade by sea. Harappan seals and beads have been found as far away as Mesopotamia.

context.text: Our knowledge comes from excavations since the 1920s at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and many other sites; Dholavira was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

vocabulary.meaning: a complex society with cities, government and culture
a channel that carries away waste water
a carved stamp used to mark goods
a place for loading and repairing boats

examples: Standard brick sizes across many cities.
Covered drains running along streets.

story.title: The City Under the Mound
story.text: Local people near Mohenjo-daro called it the "Mound of the Dead". When archaeologists dug there, they found not tombs but a city: wide streets, bathrooms in houses, wells, and drains covered with bricks. "Four and a half thousand years ago," said the archaeologist, "this city had better drains than many towns a century ago."

activities.prompt: Match the site to its feature
Harappan seals have been found in Mesopotamia.

thinking: Why would a city need good drains?
What does trade with Mesopotamia tell us about the Harappans?
speaking: Describe a Harappan city to someone as if you were walking through it.

assessment.prompt: Harappan cities had a planned grid of streets.

units.title: Mysteries of the Indus
objectives: Explain that the Indus script is undeciphered
Evaluate different theories about the decline of Harappan cities

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: A Script No One Can Read
objectives: Explain that the Indus script is undeciphered
Evaluate different theories about the decline of Harappan cities
explanation: The Harappans used signs on seals and pottery — the Indus script. Despite many attempts, no one has deciphered it. The inscriptions are very short, and no bilingual text (like the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian) has been found.
Seals often show animals, such as a one-horned animal sometimes called a "unicorn", bulls and elephants, with a few signs.

Around 1900 BCE, the large cities declined. Possible reasons include changes in rivers, drying climate and weakened monsoons, and shifts in trade. Most scholars think several factors combined; older ideas of a sudden invasion are not well supported by evidence. People did not vanish — they moved and lived in smaller settlements.

context.text: Theories about the script and the decline are debated by scholars; claims to have deciphered the script have not been widely accepted.
Studies of ancient climate and river courses provide evidence for environmental change around the time of decline.

vocabulary.meaning: work out the meaning of a code or script
a carved stamp
a possible explanation based on evidence
become weaker or smaller

examples: A seal showing a "unicorn" above a short line of signs.
The Ghaggar-Hakra river system drying over time.

story.title: The Puzzle with Missing Pieces
story.text: Professor Hoot gave the class a puzzle: short strings of symbols, no translation. "Try to read it," he said. They tried for an hour and couldn't. "Now you know how scholars feel about the Indus script," he smiled. "Sometimes the honest answer in history is: we don't know yet."

activities.prompt: Why is the script hard to decipher?
options: inscriptions are short and no bilingual text is known

activities.prompt: Most scholars think several factors caused the decline of Harappan cities.

thinking: Why is "we don't know yet" an important answer in history?
What evidence might help decipher the script?
speaking: Explain two theories about the Harappan decline and the evidence for each.

lessons.title: Gifts of the Rivers
objectives: Explain why early civilisations grew near rivers
Compare features of four river civilisations
explanation: Early civilisations grew along great rivers, which provided water, fertile soil from floods, fish and routes for travel and trade.

Mesopotamia ("land between rivers") grew between the Tigris and Euphrates in present-day Iraq. Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile, whose yearly floods left rich soil. Early Chinese civilisation grew along the Yellow River (Huang He). The Indus civilisation grew along the Indus and nearby rivers.
All four developed cities, specialised jobs, trade and systems of writing or record-keeping, but each had its own culture, beliefs and government.

context.text: Archaeological and textual evidence shows urban societies in Mesopotamia and Egypt from around the late 4th millennium BCE, the Indus from around 2600 BCE, and Shang China from around 1600 BCE.

vocabulary.meaning: the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
good for growing crops
flat land beside a river that floods
work done by people trained in one skill

examples: The Nile floods made Egyptian farming possible.
Mesopotamian scribes kept records on clay tablets.

story.title: Four Rivers, Four Peoples
story.text: Nova laid out a map with four blue lines: the Tigris–Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus and the Yellow River. "Why are the first cities all here?" she asked. The class answered together: "Water, good soil, fish and boats!" "Exactly," said Nova. "Rivers were the first highways and the first farms."

activities.prompt: Match the civilisation to its river
Why did civilisations grow near rivers?

thinking: What dangers did rivers also bring?
Why are many modern cities still near rivers?
speaking: Compare two river civilisations for someone using a map.

units.title: The Invention of Writing
objectives: Describe early writing systems
Explain why writing was important

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Marks That Speak
objectives: Describe early writing systems
Explain why writing was important
explanation: Writing began as a way to keep records: counting grain, animals and taxes. In Mesopotamia, around 3200 BCE, people pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay — cuneiform.

Egyptians developed hieroglyphs, picture-like signs, carved on monuments and written on papyrus. In China, early characters appear on oracle bones from the Shang dynasty. In India, after the Indus script, the Brahmi script (seen in Ashoka's edicts, 3rd century BCE) became the ancestor of many South and Southeast Asian scripts, including Devanagari.
Writing let people keep laws, stories, science and history — and let us hear voices from thousands of years ago.

context.text: The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE), with the same text in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, helped Jean-François Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

vocabulary.meaning: wedge-shaped writing from Mesopotamia
a picture-like sign in Egyptian writing
paper-like material made from a reed
an ancient Indian script, ancestor of many modern scripts

examples: A clay tablet recording barley rations.
Ashoka's edicts in Brahmi script.

story.title: The Stone with Three Scripts
story.text: In 1799, soldiers found a stone near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) in Egypt carved with the same message in three scripts. Because scholars could read the Greek, Jean-François Champollion eventually cracked the hieroglyphs in 1822. Suddenly, thousands of years of Egyptian writing could speak again.

activities.prompt: Match the script to its civilisation

options: keeping records like grain and taxes

activities.prompt: Brahmi is an ancestor of Devanagari.

thinking: How would life be different without writing?
Why might the Indus script still be undeciphered while hieroglyphs were cracked?
speaking: Show someone your name in a pretend cuneiform or hieroglyph style and explain the system.

lessons.title: Athens and Rome
objectives: Describe Athenian democracy and Roman government
Evaluate their legacies and limitations
explanation: In Athens (5th century BCE), male citizens took part directly in an assembly that made decisions — an early form of democracy. Women, enslaved people and foreigners were excluded, so it was far from democracy for all.
Greek thinkers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, and mathematicians like Euclid and Archimedes, shaped philosophy and science.

Rome began as a republic with elected officials and a Senate, then became an empire ruled by emperors. Romans built roads, aqueducts and a legal system whose ideas influenced later laws in many countries.

context.text: Athenian democracy is documented in ancient texts and inscriptions; historians estimate that adult male citizens were a minority of Athens' total population.
Historians debate how "democratic" Athens was given the exclusion of most residents.

vocabulary.meaning: direct participation of male citizens in decisions
a state where power is held by elected representatives
many lands ruled by one power
a channel carrying water over long distances

examples: Roman roads, some still in use.
Greek geometry studied in schools today.

story.title: Who Could Vote in Athens?
story.text: In Athens, a potter named Nikias walked to the assembly to vote on a new law. His wife, the enslaved man who worked in his shop and his neighbour from another city could not. "Athens gave the world the word democracy," Professor Hoot said, "but it took more than two thousand years to include everyone."

pairs: early direct democracy for male citizens

activities.prompt: Who was excluded from Athenian democracy?

thinking: Was Athens really a democracy? Explain your view.

speaking: Compare Athenian democracy with Indian democracy today.

lessons.title: Along the Silk Road
objectives: Describe major classical empires of Asia
Explain how trade routes connected civilisations
explanation: Classical Asia had great empires: the Achaemenid Persian Empire (6th–4th century BCE), Han China (206 BCE–220 CE), and in India the Mauryan Empire (c. 322–185 BCE) and later the Gupta Empire (c. 4th–6th century CE).

Trade routes, often called the Silk Road on land and maritime routes by sea, linked China, India, Persia, Central Asia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, cotton, glass, horses and ideas travelled along them.
Ideas travelled too: Buddhism spread from India to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan; Indian numerals and astronomy reached Persia and beyond; Roman coins have been found in southern India.

context.text: Hoards of Roman coins found in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, and Greek and Roman texts describing Indian ports, show trade between India and the Roman world.
The term "Silk Road" was coined in the 19th century; historians emphasise it was a network of many routes rather than one road.

vocabulary.meaning: a network of trade routes linking Asia and Europe
related to the sea
many regions ruled by one power
giving and receiving

examples: Chinese pilgrims like Faxian and Xuanzang travelled to India to study Buddhism.
Pepper from Kerala shipped to Rome.

story.title: Xuanzang's Journey
story.text: In the 7th century CE, the Chinese monk Xuanzang crossed deserts and mountains to India to study Buddhist texts. He stayed for years, studied at Nalanda, and returned with hundreds of manuscripts. His travel account is still one of historians' key sources about India at that time.

units.title: Human Origins

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Out of Africa
objectives: Summarise evidence for the origin and spread of Homo sapiens
Evaluate different types of evidence
explanation: Fossils show that Homo sapiens (modern humans) evolved in Africa; some of the oldest known fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old.

Genetic and archaeological evidence suggests that groups of modern humans dispersed out of Africa, with a major expansion roughly 50,000–70,000 years ago, eventually reaching South Asia, Australia, Europe and the Americas. Earlier hominins such as Homo erectus had also left Africa much earlier.

Modern humans met and sometimes interbred with other human groups like Neanderthals and Denisovans; traces of their DNA exist in many people today. Exact routes and dates are still actively researched.

context.text: The broad "recent African origin" model is supported by fossil, archaeological and genetic evidence; details of timing and routes are debated.
Many religious traditions have their own accounts of human creation; scientific evidence addresses how humans evolved, while questions of meaning are explored in faith and philosophy.

vocabulary.meaning: humans and their close extinct relatives
modern humans
preserved remains of ancient life
genetic material recovered from old remains

examples: Stone tools in India dated to hundreds of thousands of years ago, made by earlier hominins.
Neanderthal DNA traces in many living people outside Africa.

story.title: The Family Tree in Our Genes
story.text: Scientists compared DNA from people around the world and found that African populations hold the most genetic diversity — a sign that humans lived there longest. Every person alive today, they concluded, shares ancestors who once lived in Africa.

activities.prompt: Some of the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils are about…

thinking: Why does it matter that all humans share African ancestors?
Why do scientists keep revising dates and routes?
speaking: Explain the out-of-Africa model, including what remains uncertain.

lessons.title: Why Did States Form?
objectives: Explain factors in the rise of complex societies
Evaluate competing theories with archaeological evidence
explanation: Farming produced surplus food, allowing some people to specialise as potters, priests, soldiers and rulers. Populations grew, villages became towns, and some towns became cities.

With cities came social hierarchy, monumental buildings, record-keeping and often centralised authority — states. Scholars propose different drivers: irrigation management, trade, warfare, religion, or combinations.

The Indus Valley is intriguing: its cities show planning and standardisation but little clear evidence of palaces or kings, leading to debate about how it was organised. Archaeology helps test theories against evidence.

context.text: Theories of state formation (hydraulic, trade, conflict, ideological) each fit some cases better than others; scholars debate their relative importance.
Indus sites show standardised weights and bricks across a large area, but excavations have not revealed obvious royal palaces or tombs.

vocabulary.meaning: more than is needed for immediate use
people doing specific jobs
a ranking of people by status or power
a political organisation governing a territory

examples: Granaries suggesting stored surplus.
Monumental temples or ziggurats in Mesopotamia.

story.title: The City Without a King?
story.text: At Mohenjo-daro, archaeologists searched for a palace or royal tomb, as found in Egypt or Mesopotamia. Instead, they found public structures, standard bricks, drains and seals — but no grand palace. "Maybe power was shared, or organised differently," one suggested. "Or maybe we haven't found it yet."

activities.prompt: Scholars debate how the Indus cities were governed.

thinking: Is complexity always "progress"? What was lost?
What evidence would show who ruled an ancient city?
speaking: Debate which theory of state formation best fits one civilisation.

steps: Choose two early civilisations

assessment.prompt: Theories of state formation are debated.

options: coordinated systems across a wide area
